title: Bakewell Tart
subtitle: almond frangipane over raspberry jam in shortcrust
excerpt: Bakewell tart is a shortcrust pastry case filled with raspberry jam and a soft almond frangipane, baked until golden. It is one of the most recognisable British tarts, with a crisp base and a moist, nutty filling. Serves 8.
sourceNotes: The Bakewell tart as the British public now knows it, shortcrust with jam and almond frangipane, is a 20th-century commercial standardisation of the older Bakewell Pudding. The original pudding, recorded in Derbyshire from the 1820s onward, was a flaky or puff-pastry case filled with egg-and-butter custard over jam, not frangipane. Mrs Beeton (1861, Project Gutenberg #10136) gives a custard-style version. The almond-and-butter frangipane filling that defines the tart as it is commonly sold today was popularised via Derbyshire bakeries through the early 20th century. The word tart rather than pudding marks the shift to shortcrust and a cooled, sliceable format.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the baked tart, whole or in slices, wrapped well. Thaw at room temperature for two hours.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pastry case can be blind-baked a day ahead. The assembled and baked tart keeps well for two days at room temperature.

glossaryTerms.definition: A soft baked filling made from ground almonds, butter, eggs, and sugar. It swells slightly in the oven and sets to a moist, nutty sponge.
Pre-baking a pastry case before filling it. The case is lined with parchment and filled with baking beans or rice to hold the sides in place while it cooks.

content.text: Bakewell tart has a crisp shortcrust case, a layer of raspberry jam, and a soft almond filling baked until lightly golden. The filling is called
frangipane
: butter, sugar, ground almonds, and eggs beaten together. It rises just a little in the oven and settles as it cools into a moist, dense sponge with a slight crust on top.
The pastry needs to be
blind baked

before the filling goes in, otherwise the base stays soft under the jam. Give the case 20 minutes with baking beans, then 5 minutes without, until the base is dry and just starting to colour. The frangipane goes in warm or at room temperature.
What you need
Use a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin. Baking beans (or raw rice or dried lentils) are needed for
blind baking
Method
Make and chill the pastry
Rub {{plain-flour}} of plain flour (the pastry portion) with {{unsalted-butter}} of cold cubed butter until the mixture looks like coarse breadcrumbs. Stir in {{icing-sugar}} of icing sugar.
Add the egg yolk and 2 tablespoons of cold water. Bring the dough together quickly without overworking. Flatten into a disc, wrap, and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Line the tin and blind bake

Heat the oven to 175°C fan (195°C conventional). Roll the pastry out on a lightly floured surface to about 3 mm thick. Line the tart tin, pressing into the edges. Trim the excess. Prick the base with a fork. Refrigerate for another 15 minutes.
Line the case with baking parchment and fill with baking beans. Blind bake for 20 minutes. Remove the parchment and beans and bake for a further 5 to 8 minutes until the base is dry and pale golden.
Make the frangipane and fill

Beat {{unsalted-butter}} of softened butter (the frangipane portion) with {{caster-sugar}} of caster sugar until pale and light, about 3 minutes with an electric mixer. Add {{eggs}} eggs one at a time, beating after each.
Fold in {{almond-flour}} of ground almonds, 2 tablespoons of plain flour, and {{vanilla-extract}} of vanilla extract. Stir until just combined.

Spread {{raspberry-jam}} of raspberry jam in an even layer over the pastry base. Spoon the frangipane on top and spread gently to cover the jam. Scatter {{almonds-flaked}} of flaked almonds over the surface.

Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the frangipane is golden, set at the edges, and just firm at the centre. A skewer inserted in the middle should come out clean. Cool in the tin for 15 minutes before unmoulding.

items.cause: Blind baking not long enough, or jam spread onto a warm pastry case
items.fix: Make sure the base is dry before filling. Let the baked case cool slightly before adding jam. Use a jam that is not too wet.
Reduce temperature by 10°C and tent with foil if the top is browning faster than the centre is setting.

items.symptom: Filling does not set in the centre
items.fix: Give it another 5 to 10 minutes. The skewer test is reliable: it must come out clean.

items.symptom: Pastry shrinks down the sides during blind baking
items.cause: Pastry not rested long enough, or stretched when lining the tin
items.fix: Chill the lined tin again before baking, and ease the pastry gently into the tin rather than stretching it.

content.text: Where this dish lives

The town of Bakewell in Derbyshire has been associated with this sweet tart since the early 20th century. The tart differs from the older Bakewell pudding: that was a flaky-pastry case with a poured custard, not a frangipane. The tart version, with its shortcrust base and almond filling, became the national standard through bakeries and tearooms. It is best the day after baking, when the pastry has settled and the frangipane has firmed to its proper dense, nutty slice.
